## Sound memory: recordings and archives to ensure we never forget

In the pockets of half of Almuñécar, an involuntary archive already slumbers. These are handheld mobile phone recordings, with the levante wind sneaking into the microphone, where a death knell or a festive peal gets trapped between the noise of a motorbike and a child's voice. No one has cataloged them, no one has requested them, but they exist. They are the spontaneous sound memory of a town that senses something is slipping away and, without quite knowing why, decides to save it in the phone's gallery right next to the photos of Sunday's paella.

The municipal archive, on the other hand, holds material of a different nature. There rest reel-to-reel tapes from the seventies with recordings of peals that no one plays anymore, recordings made when mechanization had not yet silenced the bell towers. The problem is that these tapes are degrading in cardboard boxes, without a digitization plan to rescue them before the magnetic rust swallows them forever. There is no allocated budget, no responsible technician, no schedule of action. Only the certainty that with each passing year, the tape loses a little more of its ability to return that sound to us.

The paradox is cruel: Almuñécar preserves sound testimonies from the seventies while letting the current peals, the last manual ones, fade away without systematic recording. The locals record in snippets, with the best of intentions, but without documentary criteria. What is missing is someone to note the date, the festival, the name of the bell ringer, the meaning of the peal. What is missing is someone to ask why that peal has three dry strokes at the end or why that toll stretches longer than usual. Without that data, the recording is just beautiful noise; with it, it becomes an ethnographic document.

The model that could light the way is in León. The bell ringers of that province have built a sound archive with over five hundred recordings, a collection that is not limited to storing audio but contextualizes it, dates it, and links it to the names of those who performed it. That archive was not born of an institution or a European project: it was born of the obstinacy of a few men and women who understood that every lost peal is a word going extinct. Five hundred recordings may seem few compared to the immensity of the peninsular heritage, but they are five hundred more than Almuñécar has.

Current technology would allow this model to be replicated at a reduced cost. A mid-range phone, a twenty-euro lavalier microphone, and an account on a digital repository would be enough to get started. What is lacking is not money, but the decision to do it. What is lacking is for someone in the City Council to understand that digitizing a 1974 tape is not a whim of nostalgics, but a cultural rescue operation as urgent as restoring a retable or shoring up a city wall. Sound is also heritage, even if it does not take up space in display cases or feature in tourist guides.

The Sexitan bell ringers who still climb the bell tower are not eternal. Some are over seventy years old, and their hands, though steady, are beginning to falter during long peals. When they are gone, no one will be able to explain why the toll for the souls is played with that slow, almost dragging cadence that mimics the pace of a funeral procession. Current recordings, taken without method, will not suffice to reconstruct that knowledge. What will be needed is the archive that does not exist today, the project that no one has launched, the will that is delayed while the tapes from the seventies quietly fall apart.

There is a scene that repeats itself on the terraces of the Town Hall square when the bell tower rings. Tourists look up, smile, record ten seconds on their phones, and go back to eating. Those ten seconds, multiplied by hundreds of visitors each summer, form a chaotic and scattered archive that will never be consulted. Meanwhile, the municipal archive holds tapes that no one digitizes, and the bell ringers of León demonstrate that systematic work is possible. Almuñécar has the raw materials: it has the sounds, it has the informants, it has the technology. It just lacks the basket.

Time is running out, and not just because of the bell ringers' age. The reel-to-reel tapes from the seventies have a limited lifespan, and every playback without the proper conditions accelerates their deterioration. If their digitization is not addressed in the coming years, the last manual toll of Almuñécar could be reduced to a hazy memory in the minds of the elderly, without any physical medium to preserve it for future generations. A town's sound memory should not depend on the luck of a mobile phone or the endurance of a tape forgotten in a drawer.
